name: Successful Adoption Factors
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Pattern Behind Every Blockchain Project That Actually Shipped
lesson.summary: Pulling together the case studies from the previous chapters, a small set of recurring factors, real multi-party mistrust, a forcing function that makes participation non-optional, a dominant player who can mandate adoption, and a narrow scope, separate the blockchain projects that reached lasting production use from the ones that quietly died.
lesson.body:
This chapter is a synthesis, not a new case study. It looks back across supply chain, healthcare, financial services, e-commerce, and retail, at the projects that reached durable production use, MediLedger, JPM Coin and Onyx, Carrefour and Walmart-style food traceability, AURA, and at the projects that did not, TradeLens, we.trade, OpenBazaar, Diem, and most retail NFT loyalty programs, and asks what actually separated one group from the other. Four factors show up again and again.

The first factor is genuine multi-party mistrust that a single company's internal database cannot solve. This is the baseline condition the blockchain definition itself points to. JPM Coin barely needed it, since it mostly connects JPMorgan to its own institutional clients rather than a wide set of independent competitors, which is part of why critics can fairly describe it as closer to a well-designed private database than a true decentralized system. MediLedger and Carrefour's traceability work needed it more, since many genuinely independent companies had to agree to a shared record without any one of them controlling it.

The second factor is a forcing function that makes participation non-optional. Regulation forced pharmaceutical companies to build real, working drug verification systems on a legal deadline under the Drug Supply Chain Security Act. A dominant customer, Walmart, forced its leafy-green suppliers onto a traceability system by making it a condition of doing business. Compare that with we.trade and TradeLens, which each asked a group of competing companies to voluntarily commit real investment to shared infrastructure with no law and no dominant customer requiring it, and in both cases participation stalled out.

The third factor, closely related, is whether a single actor had enough market power to set the standard, rather than the project depending on a flat consortium of equals reaching consensus. Walmart could simply mandate supplier participation. Maersk, despite being the largest container shipping line in the world, could not compel its rivals the same way, because TradeLens looked and functioned like Maersk's own platform rather than neutral, jointly-owned industry infrastructure, and competitors were unwilling to build critical operations on top of it.

The fourth factor is scope. The projects that lasted tended to target one specific, well-bounded workflow, MediLedger targets a defined compliance verification step, Carrefour's system targets traceability for a defined set of product categories, rather than attempting to replace an entire industry's infrastructure all at once. TradeLens tried to digitize the full global shipping documentation stack in one project; Diem tried to introduce a new global currency instrument in one project. Bigger ambition meant more parties who had to agree, more ways for the project to stall, and more attention from regulators and competitors who saw a threat rather than a convenience.

Put together, the honest overall pattern looks less like decentralization as an end in itself and more like this: a shared, tamper-evident record among a small number of known, semi-trusted institutions, brought together by a real legal or contractual reason they cannot avoid, working on one clearly defined problem. That is a much narrower and more boring description than the sweeping claims that defined blockchain's Peak of Inflated Expectations, but it is the description that actually matches the projects still running today.
